title: Analysis of Data
summary: After data are collected, edited and presented, they are analysed to draw out the important facts. The first step is to find one representative value for the whole data, called the average or measure of central tendency.

Central tendency is the tendency of data to cluster around a central value. An average is a single figure, typical of all the items, that the mind can grasp quickly. Example: Sachin scores 59, 78, 100, 50 and 63 in five innings, a total of 350, so his average is 350 ÷ 5 = 70, though he never scored exactly 70.
## Purpose and functions of an average
(1) It sums up raw data in brief. (2) It makes comparison between groups easy. (3) It gives a single representative value. (4) It helps in planning future policy and programmes.
There are various measures of central tendency, and the arithmetic mean is one of them. The arithmetic mean is the sum of the items divided by the number of items: X̄ = Σx ÷ N.
Example: the marks 4, 6, 3, 7, 8, 2, 5 add up to 35, and 35 ÷ 7 = 5. A weekly use of 2.1 kg gives 2.1 ÷ 7 = 0.3 kg a day, so 3 kg in 10 days.
Individual series. Direct method: X̄ = Σx ÷ N. Short-cut (assumed mean) method: X̄ = A + Σd ÷ N, where d = x − A.
Discrete series. Direct method: X̄ = Σfx ÷ Σf. Short-cut method: X̄ = A + Σfd ÷ Σf. Example: children per family 0–6 with f 13, 17, 20, 40, 20, 17, 13 gives Σfx = 420 and N = 140, so X̄ = 3.

Continuous series: first find the mid-values, x = (lower limit + upper limit) ÷ 2. Then use one of three methods: direct, X̄ = Σfx ÷ N; short-cut, X̄ = A + Σfd ÷ N; or step deviation, X̄ = A + (Σfd′ ÷ N) × c, where d′ = (x − A) ÷ c and c is the common class width.

Worked example (step deviation): class intervals 0–10 … 40–50 with f 20, 40, 10, 5, 25. The mid-values are 5, 15, 25, 35, 45. Take A = 25 and c = 10, so d′ = −2, −1, 0, 1, 2 and fd′ = −40, −40, 0, 5, 50, giving Σfd′ = −25. Then X̄ = 25 + (−25 ÷ 100) × 10 = 25 − 2.5 = 22.5.

(1) The mean is a theoretical value that may not exist in fact. 27 children in 10 families gives an average of 2.7 children, which is impossible for any one family. (2) The mean cannot be found for qualitative data such as honesty, bravery or beauty.

vsa: Explain the concept of central tendency.
Central tendency is the tendency of data to cluster around a central value. The average (e.g. the arithmetic mean) measures it and gives one representative value for the whole data.
State the purpose of an average.
An average gives a single value representative of all the items. It sums up large data briefly, makes comparison between groups easy, and helps in framing policy.

or: State two functions of an average.

(1) It presents raw data briefly in one representative figure.
(2) It makes comparison between two or more groups easy.

vsa: Write the short-cut (assumed mean) formula for the arithmetic mean.
X̄ = A + Σfd ÷ N, where A is the assumed mean, d = x − A, f is the frequency and N = Σf. For an individual series, X̄ = A + Σd ÷ N.
How is the arithmetic mean obtained?
Add all the items and divide by the number of items: X̄ = Σx ÷ N. Example: 50 marks scored by 10 students gives a mean of 5.

or: What is a discrete series? Give an example.

A discrete series shows exact (separate) values of a variable with their frequencies.
Example: marks 30, 40, 50, 60, 70 with 4, 6, 10, 20, 10 students.
It is used for discrete variables such as the number of children per family.

sa: What is central tendency? State two precautions in using the arithmetic mean.

Central tendency is the tendency of data to cluster around a central value, measured by an average.
Precautions: (1) The mean is a theoretical value that may not exist in fact — 2.7 children per family is impossible for any one family. (2) The mean cannot be used for qualitative data such as honesty or beauty.
